specAnchors.text: know that alkenes contain the functional group >C=C<
know the general formula for alkenes
explain why alkenes are classified as unsaturated hydrocarbons

understand how to draw the structural and displayed formulae for alkenes with up to four carbon atoms in the molecule, and name the unbranched-chain isomers knowledge of cis/trans or E/Z notation is not required

primer.text: From Halogens & Alkanes you already know how the saturated family swaps atoms under UV light. This note introduces its double-bonded cousins: the C=C functional group, the alkane-versus-alkene formula difference, and why that open double bond makes alkenes so much more reactive.

modules.title: The C=C functional group family
modules.opening: Alkenes are the unsaturated counterpart to alkanes, defined by one structural feature. This lesson identifies the C=C functional group, generates the family formula, and explains what unsaturated really means.
keyPoints: Alkenes are unsaturated hydrocarbons whose functional group is the C=C double bond.
The general formula of an alkene is CnH2n, two fewer hydrogens than the alkane recipe.
Unsaturated means the C=C bond can open, letting each carbon form one more single bond.
Because the double bond can open, alkenes are much more reactive than alkanes.
Each carbon of the double bond ends up with four single bonds once the incoming atoms attach.

low.restatement: Alkenes carry a carbon-carbon double bond, written C=C, and follow the formula CnH2n. The double bond can open up, which is why alkenes are called unsaturated and react more readily than alkanes.
low.analogy: An alkene is a zip half-open on a jacket: the open teeth are ready to fasten onto something new, while the fully zipped alkane has no spare grip.
low.examPointer: Write the functional group as C=C when asked, and contrast the CnH2n formula with the alkane CnH2n+2.

medium.restatement: Every alkene contains the C=C functional group, the double bond that defines the family and follows the general formula CnH2n. Unsaturated describes the two spare bonding capacities at that bond: opening it lets an incoming atom bond to each carbon, converting one double and two singles into four single bonds per carbon pair.
medium.analogy: Think of the double bond as a two-person handshake with arms linked twice; guests arriving can undo one link so each host greets a new visitor with a firm single grip.
medium.examPointer: Explain reactivity through the openable double bond, then show the formula difference from alkanes by comparing CnH2n with CnH2n+2.

modules.title: Drawing and naming the first four
modules.opening: The first four alkenes carry position numbers in their names because the double bond can sit in different places. This lesson lines up ethene to pent-1-ene and reads the numbering system.
keyPoints: The first members are ethene C2H4, propene C3H6, but-1-ene C4H8 and pent-1-ene C5H10.
Names of longer alkenes carry a number showing where the C=C bond begins in the chain.
In pent-2-ene the double bond sits between the second and third carbon atoms.
Drawing a displayed alkene means every bond shown, with the double bond drawn as two lines.
The cis/trans and E/Z naming systems stay outside the requirement, which covers unbranched-chain isomers only.

low.restatement: Learn ethene, propene, but-1-ene and pent-1-ene with formulae C2H4 to C5H10. The number in the name says which carbon the double bond starts at, counted from one end.
low.analogy: The name works like a street address for the double bond: ethene and propene live in tiny houses with one possible door, but from butene onward the number tells you which door is open.
low.examPointer: Practise drawing each displayed formula with the double bond as two clear lines; both carbons still show four bonds in total.

medium.restatement: The table runs ethene C2H4, propene C3H6, but-1-ene C4H8 and pent-1-ene C5H10, each obeying CnH2n with one C=C. Position numbers count from the nearer end, so pent-2-ene places the double bond between carbons two and three, and only unbranched-chain isomers are named at this level.
medium.analogy: Longer alkene names are like hotel room numbers: the stem names the building size and the number tells you the floor where the double-bond event happens.
medium.examPointer: Count from the end that gives the lower number, and remember cis/trans and E/Z labels are outside the requirement.

glossary.definition: An unsaturated hydrocarbon of the family with general formula CnH2n and one C=C double bond.
Describing a hydrocarbon whose C=C double bond can open to add more atoms.
A bond made of two shared electron pairs between two carbon atoms, written C=C.
The family recipe using n; for alkenes it is CnH2n.
A straight-chain arrangement of a molecular formula, the only isomer type named at this level.
